feedback: If a learner writes 'same thing, just with better gear', prompt: the main GOAL changed — Heroic-Age expeditions did some science, but their headline aim was often to be first and survive, while today's work is centred on research questions. Point to the purpose row and ask what each team was mainly trying to find out.
If a learner says modern polar work is 'easy sightseeing', note it is demanding scientific research, especially measuring climate change in harsh conditions.
If a learner lists tools but cannot link them to survival or measurement, ask: 'What exactly does a heated station / GPS / ice-core drill let a scientist do that furs and a sextant could not?'
Affirm answers that name BOTH a tool change and a question change, e.g. 'satellites let scientists measure ice across the whole continent, so they can ask how fast it is melting.'
activities.intendedInsight: Polar exploration did not end with the Heroic Age; it continued and changed. Better tools both reduce danger AND change the questions science can ask — from reaching a place to understanding a system.
learnerActions: Study paired images or descriptions of a 1911 polar expedition and a present-day research station.
Fill in a four-row comparison table across: PURPOSE, TECHNOLOGY, DANGER, and WHO TAKES PART.
For PURPOSE, write the 1911 goal (e.g. 'reach the Pole first and survive — national glory') beside the modern goal (e.g. 'measure the ice and understand the climate').
For TECHNOLOGY, list then-tools (sextant, dog teams, wooden ship, furs) beside now-tools (GPS/satellites, icebreaker, ice-core drill, heated station, aircraft).
For DANGER, note the high fatality of the Heroic Age versus greatly reduced risk today, and say which modern tool most reduces a given risk.
For WHO TAKES PART, contrast small, mostly nationally organised all-male parties with today's diverse international teams including women scientists.
Write one sentence answering: 'What changed most — the tools or the question?'
activities.title: Then vs Now: a four-dimension comparison

feedback: If a learner assumes 'explorers were all men' or all from one country, introduce the glaciologist and marine-biologist profiles and note teams today are international and diverse.
If a learner cannot name a modern scientist, revisit a profile card before moving on.
Reward answers that contrast the scientist's research mission with an explorer's race-to-be-first goal.
activities.intendedInsight: Today's polar teams are international and diverse and include leading women scientists; the work is science-driven, which is a sharp contrast to the small national, all-male parties of the Heroic Age.
learnerActions: Read or role-play a short profile/interview with a modern scientist — e.g. a glaciologist who reads climate records from ice cores, or a marine biologist studying the Southern Ocean.
Write or speak three questions you would ask about what that scientist studies and how.
Compare that scientist's stated mission with a Heroic-Age explorer's goal, writing one sentence on how they differ.
Name at least one modern polar scientist and say what field that scientist works in.
activities.title: Interview a modern polar scientist

feedback: If a learner explains Heroic-Age deaths as 'weakness' or Amundsen's success as 'luck', redirect to the planning and technology differences (dogs and preparation vs man-hauling).
If a learner sorts correctly but gives no 'what it lets you do' reason, prompt for the function of each tool.
The sorting step checks recognition of era and tool function but does not by itself elicit explanation; have learners then give a spoken or written reason so they go beyond matching to reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Differences between eras come from technology, methods and planning, not from early explorers being weak or modern ones being merely lucky.
learnerActions: Given a mixed set of items (sextant, GPS unit, dog harness, ice-core drill, fur parka, satellite phone, wooden ship, icebreaker), sort each into THEN or NOW.
For each NOW item, state one thing it lets a scientist do or survive that the matching THEN item could not.
Explain why Amundsen's careful planning and use of dogs is a method/planning difference, not just luck, compared with Scott's man-hauling — using the equipment as evidence.
activities.title: Kit out the expedition: then and now
